title: Relativistic Addition of Velocities
short_intro: The addition of velocities is the kinematic relation used to determine the velocity of an object in one inertial frame given its velocity in another frame. In special relativity, it modifies the classical Galilean transformation to preserve the invariance of the speed of light.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Galilean velocity addition in classical mechanics, relative velocity in one and two dimensions, and frame of reference concepts.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Einstein's relativistic velocity addition formula, length contraction and time dilation implications, and Fizeau's water-tube experiment.

prerequisites: Inertial and non-inertial frames of reference

concept_notes.heading: Galilean Velocity Addition
bullets: In classical mechanics, velocities simply add vectorially according to u = v + u'.
Assumes absolute time where intervals dt are identical in all inertial frames.
Fails at speeds approaching the speed of light c because it allows resultant velocities to exceed c.

concept_notes.heading: Postulates of Special Relativity
bullets: The laws of physics are invariant in all inertial reference frames.
The speed of light in vacuum c is isotropic and independent of the motion of the source or observer.
Requires the abandonment of absolute simultaneity and the adoption of Lorentz transformations.

concept_notes.heading: Relativistic Velocity Addition Formula
bullets: Derived by taking differentials of the Lorentz coordinate transformations x' = γ(x - vt) and t' = γ(t - vx/c²).
Ensures that the composition of any velocity less than c with another velocity less than c never equals or exceeds c.
Reduces to the classical Galilean expression when the relative velocity v is much smaller than c.

concept_notes.heading: Fizeau's Experiment on Ether Drag
bullets: Measured the speed of light in flowing water to test the Fresnel dragging coefficient.
Provided historical empirical support for the relativistic velocity addition formula before Einstein's formulation.
Demonstrated that moving media do not simply add their velocity to light linearly.

derivations.title: Galilean Velocity Addition
steps: Consider position coordinate relation x = x' + vt between two frames S and S'.
Take the time derivative of the position relation assuming dt = dt'.
Obtain the velocity relation dx/dt = dx'/dt' + v.

derivations.title: Relativistic Velocity Addition
derivations.conditions: Inertial frames S and S' moving with relative velocity v along the x-axis
steps: Start with the differential Lorentz transformations: dx' = gamma(dx - v dt) and dt' = gamma(dt - v dx / c^2).
Express the velocity in frame S' as u_x' = dx' / dt' = gamma(dx - v dt) / [gamma(dt - v dx / c^2)].
Divide numerator and denominator by dt, substituting u_x = dx/dt to get u_x' = (u_x - v) / (1 - v u_x / c^2).
Invert to solve for u_x in terms of u_x': u_x = (u_x' + v) / (1 + v u_x' / c^2).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Addition Asymptotic Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of resultant velocity u_x versus source velocity u_x' for various frame velocities v, bounded strictly between -c and +c.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that regardless of how high u_x' and v are, the sum never crosses the horizontal asymptote at u_x = c.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting asymptotic behavior and upper speed limits in PGT conceptual questions.

solved_numericals.question: A train is moving at 60 km/h east relative to the ground. A passenger walks inside the train at 5 km/h east relative to the train. Find the velocity of the passenger relative to the ground.
solution_steps: Identify velocities in classical framework: v = 60 km/h, u' = 5 km/h.
Apply Galilean velocity addition: u = u' + v.

solved_numericals.question: Two spaceships approach each other, each moving at a speed of 0.8c relative to a stationary observer on Earth. What is the speed of one spaceship relative to the other?
solution_steps: Let frame S be Earth. Spaceship 1 moves at v = -0.8c. Spaceship 2 moves at u_x = 0.8c in Earth frame.
We need the velocity u_x' of spaceship 2 relative to spaceship 1.
Use inverse relativistic formula: u_x' = (u_x - v) / (1 - v u_x / c^2).

solved_numericals.question: A particle emits a photon in the direction of its motion. If the particle is moving at speed v = 0.6c relative to the laboratory, what is the speed of the photon in the laboratory frame?
solution_steps: Identify the speed of the photon in the particle's rest frame: u_x' = c.
Identify the velocity of the particle frame: v = 0.6c.
Apply the relativistic velocity addition formula: u_x = (u_x' + v) / (1 + v u_x' / c^2).
Substitute c for u_x': u_x = (c + 0.6c) / (1 + (0.6c * c) / c^2).

assumptions_and_limitations: Formulas assume motion restricted to collinear directions (standard configuration). Transverse components require separate transformation equations involving the Lorentz factor gamma.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Velocities simply add as u = u' + v even at speeds close to the speed of light.
common_misconceptions.correct: Velocities must combine via the relativistic relation u = (u' + v)/(1 + vu'/c^2).
common_misconceptions.why: Linear addition permits speeds greater than c, which violates the second postulate of special relativity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The speed of light changes when measured from a moving inertial frame.
common_misconceptions.correct: The speed of light c is invariant in all inertial frames.
common_misconceptions.why: Einstein's postulate states that c is constant regardless of the relative motion of source and observer.

quick_revision: Relativistic velocity addition guarantees that no material object or signal can exceed the speed of light c.
Classical Velocity Addition: u = u' + v
Relativistic Velocity Addition (x-component): u_x = \frac{u_x' + v}{1 + \frac{v u_x'}{c^2}}
